description: Postcards from Space is a Phoenix team of 11th graders building a web app for the “Abandoned but not Forgotten” challenge, in which the hardware NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space writes postcards to school-age kids about what it discovered and where it is today. There’s a strong Arizona thread: UA led the Phoenix Mars Lander and runs the HiRISE camera that still photographs it, ASU’s LROC camera images Apollo hardware on the Moon, and every moonwalker trained in Flagstaff.
summary:
Postcards from Space is a bilingual web app in which the hardware NASA left behind writes kids a postcard. Sixteen machines tell their own stories in the first person, including the Apollo 11 lander and laser reflector, the Spirit, Opportunity and Sojourner rovers, the Phoenix and InSight landers, Ingenuity and both Voyagers. Each explains why it was sent, what it discovered and where it rests today.

The challenge asked for an engaging, accurate, story-driven tool for school-age space fans. Each postcard pairs the letter with real NASA and university images, including LROC (ASU) and HiRISE (UArizona) views of the hardware from orbit. Kids answer a quiz to earn a stamp in a Mission Passport, compare distances on a ladder out to interstellar space, and can have every letter read aloud, in English or Spanish.

Every fact is sourced from NASA’s NSSDCA catalog and mission pages, and an independent audit checked it. Kids mostly hear about active missions, so this turns retired machines into characters and connects them to the science they made possible.
details: Postcards from Space is a bilingual web app in which 16 pieces of hardware NASA left behind write kids a postcard. They include the Apollo 11 lander and laser reflector, the Apollo 17 rover, Surveyor 3, Spirit, Opportunity, Sojourner, Viking 1, Phoenix, InSight, Ingenuity, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer 10 and both Voyagers. Each machine explains in its own voice why it was sent, what it discovered and where it rests today. Every letter is paired with a real NASA photo and, where one exists, a view of the machine today taken from orbit. Kids answer one question per postcard to earn a stamp in their Mission Passport, see how far away each machine is on a distance scale that runs from the Moon out to interstellar space, and follow a live countdown to Voyager 1 reaching one light-day from Earth. Every letter can be read aloud, in English or Spanish. Kids mostly hear about active missions, so the app turns the retired machines that made today’s science possible into characters they’ll remember. It reaches bilingual families, and teachers can rely on it because every fact comes from NASA sources. I built it with React, TypeScript and Vite, hosted it on Vercel, and used images from the NASA Image and Video Library, NASA Photojournal, ASU’s LROC and the University of Arizona’s HiRISE, with distances from NASA JPL Horizons. Every fact is checked automatically against its NASA or NSSDCA source, and Claude (Anthropic) served as my AI coding and research assistant. The app is creative because the hardware tells its own story in a postcard style with airmail borders, perforated stamps and postmarks, and the passport turns learning into a collection. I prioritized accuracy: disputed details are left out, and an independent audit checked every sentence, with the two it flagged fixed. I also wrote for kids aged 8 to 12, made it keyboard-, screen-reader- and read-aloud-friendly with a Lighthouse accessibility score of 100, and highlighted Arizona’s role through the Phoenix lander, the HiRISE and LROC cameras, and Apollo astronaut training near Flagstaff. Kids can tap any machine to “send a hello” and watch a light pulse travel to it, learning that a radio message takes 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, 12.5 minutes to reach Mars, and about a full day to reach Voyager 1. A switch relabels the scale in light travel time, and machines whose stamps they’ve collected light up.
